It holds because the price is computed the same way every time, because the four services a request passes through agree on what it was, and because the team can change any of that without breaking it. Those are the other two screens.

c4.code.body: Not drawn, and the source says why: an IDE generates it on demand, so a hand-drawn one is stale the day it is committed. The service detail on the other tab shows the real code instead, which is the same information with no second copy to maintain.
c4.code.quote: This level of detail is not recommended for anything but the most important or complex components. … particularly for long-lived documentation, because most IDEs can generate this level of detail on demand.
c4.code.title: Level 4 — Code
c4.component.body: One container, opened up: the Quotation Service, and the pieces a quotation passes through in the order it passes through them. Drawn for this container and no other, which is the guidance — a component diagram per container is a maintenance bill nobody pays twice.
c4.component.quote: Next you can zoom in and decompose a container to describe the components that reside inside it; including their responsibilities and the technology/implementation details. … only create component diagrams if you feel they add value, and consider automating their creation for long-lived documentation.
c4.component.title: Level 3 — Component
c4.container.audience: Technical people inside and outside the software development team; including software architects, developers and operations/support staff
c4.container.body: The separately deployable pieces and the technology each one is — that is what the brackets are for. Note what the definition does NOT say: nothing about Docker. The word predates it, and a database schema is a container here.
c4.container.quote: A container is an application or a data store. For example, a server-side web application, a client-side single-page application, a desktop application, a mobile app, a database schema, a folder on a file system, an Amazon Web Services S3 bucket, etc.
c4.container.title: Level 2 — Container
c4.context.audience: Everybody, both technical and non-technical people, inside and outside the software development team
c4.context.body: One box for the whole platform, the people who use it, and the systems it exchanges with. No technology at all — this is the level you can put in front of someone who does not write software.
c4.context.quote: A system context diagram is a good starting point for diagramming and documenting a software system, allowing you to step back and see the big picture. … Detail isn't important here as this is your zoomed out view showing a big picture.
c4.context.title: Level 1 — System Context
c4.hierarchy: A software system is made up of one or more containers (applications and data stores), each of which contains one or more components, which in turn are implemented by one or more code elements (classes, interfaces, objects, functions, etc).
c4.hierarchyNote: The hierarchy is the model. The diagrams are just four ways of looking at it, and C4 is deliberately notation independent and tooling independent — the boxes here could be drawn any way at all without ceasing to be C4.
c4.lede: Four levels of zoom over one static structure. The definitions below are quoted from c4model.com rather than paraphrased, because the value of a shared notation is that everyone is using the same one. Every diagram here is rendered from Mermaid source held in the page.
c4.supplementary: Beyond these four, C4 names a set of supporting diagrams — system landscape, dynamic, and deployment. The request flow on the other tab is the dynamic one; deployment is described in the platform note below rather than drawn, because this system runs in a single environment.
c4.title: The C4 model, as its author defines it
calendar.legend: Days with a price have a sailing. The window is eight weeks from the schedule's first day.
catalog.campaign-service.what: The Campaign Cohort Hub. It segments customers into cohorts from booking history and accrued TEU, decides which offer each cohort should see, and emits targeting events. It reads from the Data Platform rather than the transactional store, so audience work can never slow down booking.
catalog.campaign-service.when: A lane is running under capacity for the next sailing window. The hub identifies customers who shipped that corridor in the last two quarters but not this one, and targets a time-boxed incentive at exactly that cohort instead of discounting the lane for everyone.
catalog.data-platform.what: The relational analytics store. Booking and quotation events land here from the Legacy ERP Engine on a read replica, separated from the transactional primary so reporting load can never contend with booking writes.
catalog.data-platform.when: The Lead Product Owner (LPO) needs monthly TEU accrual per customer to check that Volume Loyalty Framework milestones are firing correctly. That query scans a quarter of history — running it against the transactional primary would put booking latency at risk, so it runs here instead.
catalog.feature-flags.what: A managed flag evaluation service. It decouples deploying code from releasing behaviour: a change ships dark, is switched on for a named slice of traffic, and can be switched off in seconds without a rollback, a redeploy, or a release window.
catalog.feature-flags.when: Rolling the Quotation Flex Cart multi-port hold out to the first 5% of Silver Sail customers. If rate-reservation latency against the Legacy ERP Engine degrades under the added load, the flag is killed immediately — the code stays deployed and nobody has to page a release engineer.
catalog.quotation-service.what: The Core Quotation Module. It resolves a lane to a base rate, prices each container row by equipment type and quantity, applies the surcharges the row earns, asks the Volume Loyalty Framework for the customer's discount, and reserves the resulting rate against the Legacy ERP Engine for a fixed validity window.
catalog.quotation-service.when: A customer requests a rate at 02:00 local time, outside any human desk's hours. The service prices the lane, holds it for 72 hours through the Quotation Flex Cart, and the customer books the next morning at the same number — no re-quote, no negotiation, no staff involved.
catalog.routing-gateway.what: A layer-7 reverse proxy sitting in front of every service. It terminates TLS, enforces per-client rate limits, routes by path prefix, injects a trace header so one request can be followed end to end, and load-balances across replicas. It is also the cluster ingress.
catalog.routing-gateway.when: The Campaign Cohort Hub launches a promotion and quote traffic spikes roughly eightfold within a minute. The gateway absorbs the burst, throttles the clients that are hammering the endpoint, and shifts traffic across healthy replicas — with no service redeploy and no code change.
catalog.translation-api.what: Lokalise, the managed localisation platform this site actually runs on. Translation keys live outside the application build, so copy is corrected in any locale without shipping a release. `scripts/pull-locales.mjs` writes the bundles before the build and the app imports them, so the running site has no runtime token and no network dependency on a translation vendor. Any key missing from a locale falls back to the base rather than rendering blank.
catalog.translation-api.when: A surcharge label reads ambiguously in one market and the local team wants it reworded before the next sailing. They edit the string in the platform, the next build picks it up, and no engineer touches the repository.
catalog.web-portal.what: The customer-facing application. It renders quotation forms and rate comparisons on the server, hydrates only the interactive parts, and holds no business rules of its own — pricing and eligibility always come from the service layer so a browser can never be the source of truth.
catalog.web-portal.when: A customer opens a rate search from a slow mobile connection in a port city. Server rendering means the first meaningful paint carries real lane data rather than a spinner, and the interactive quote form hydrates afterwards without blocking the read.
cheat.artifacts.backlog.body: The single, ordered list of everything the product might need. Owned by the PO; refined continuously so the top is ready to pull.
cheat.artifacts.increment.body: A concrete step toward the Product Goal, usable and meeting the Definition of Done. Work that does not meet it is not an increment and is not shown at the Review.
cheat.artifacts.sprintBacklog.body: What was pulled into this Sprint and the plan for delivering it. Owned by the Developers and updated throughout the Sprint.
cheat.artifacts.title: Three artifacts, each with a commitment
cheat.events.daily.body: For the Developers, by the Developers: inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adjust the day's plan. Same time and place, to keep it simple.
cheat.events.note: Shorter Sprints get proportionally shorter events; a two-week Sprint, which this team runs, plans in about four hours. Every event is an opportunity to inspect and adapt, which is why none may be skipped.
cheat.events.planning.body: Three questions: why is this Sprint valuable, what can be done, how will it get done. Ends with a Sprint Goal and a Sprint Backlog.
cheat.events.planning.box: Max 8 hours for a one-month Sprint
cheat.events.retro.body: The team inspects itself — people, process, tools, Definition of Done — and picks the most helpful changes to make in the next Sprint. Closes the Sprint.
cheat.events.retro.box: Max 3 hours for a one-month Sprint
cheat.events.review.body: Show the increment to stakeholders and inspect the outcome; decide together what to adapt next. A working session, not a presentation.
cheat.events.review.box: Max 4 hours for a one-month Sprint
cheat.events.sprint.body: The container for all other events. Fixed length, starts the moment the last one ends, no gaps. A new Sprint cannot change the Sprint Goal or lower quality; only the PO can cancel one.
cheat.events.title: Five events, and their time-boxes
cheat.lede: Three accountabilities, five events, three artifacts, three pillars, five values — as the Scrum Guide 2020 states them, with the guide's own time-boxes — and then what this team layers on top. The quiz below asks about this page.
cheat.pillars.body: Transparency, inspection, adaptation. Scrum is empirical: decisions are made on what is observed, so the work and the process must be visible, checked often, and changed when the check says so.
cheat.pillars.title: Three pillars
cheat.practices.dod.body: Here: code reviewed by two, tests green, deployed to the review environment, acceptance criteria met. The Increment's commitment, written down so nobody has to remember it.
cheat.practices.dor.body: What an item must have before it can be pulled into a Sprint: acceptance criteria, an estimate, no open questions. Not in the guide; a practice that stops half-understood work entering the Sprint.
cheat.practices.refinement.body: An ongoing activity, not an event: breaking items down, adding detail and estimates so the top of the backlog is always ready. The guide names it; the team schedules it weekly.
cheat.practices.storyPoints.body: Relative size, not hours: 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. Estimated together, so the number carries the team's shared sense of the work. The simulation on the process screen uses the same scale.
cheat.practices.title: What this team layers on the guide
cheat.quizNote: The five questions below test the two rules the quiz asks most about, the loyalty milestone, TEU, and the rate-hold service — all of which are on this page or on the business screen.
cheat.roles.devs.body: Everyone who builds the increment — on this team, designer, developers and QA alike. Cross-functional and self-managing: they decide how the work is done and hold each other to the Definition of Done.
cheat.roles.devs.owns: Own the Sprint Backlog and the Increment
cheat.roles.note: The guide calls these accountabilities, not roles, and there is no fourth. Ten or fewer people in total; typically the PO and SM are one each and the rest are Developers.
cheat.roles.po.body: One person, not a committee. Sets the Product Goal, orders the backlog, and is the one who says what the team works on next. Others may suggest; the PO decides.
cheat.roles.po.owns: Owns the Product Backlog and its value
cheat.roles.sm.body: Makes Scrum work as the guide describes it: coaches the team, removes what blocks it, keeps the events inside their time-boxes. Not a project manager, and never a desk work queues in front of.
cheat.roles.title: The Scrum Team — three accountabilities
cheat.title: Everything Scrum asks of a team, on one page.
cheat.values.body: Commitment, focus, openness, respect, courage. The pillars only hold when the people practise these; the guide says trust is built through them.
cheat.values.title: Five values

home.expertise.body: Port to port. One quotation fixes three things for 72 hours — space on a ship, a price, and a departure date — and the booking, the paperwork and the delivery all hang off it. This site takes that one quotation apart: how the price is worked out, what runs behind it, and how the work of building it is organised.
home.expertise.title:
One quotation,
end to end
home.hero.title:
From a quote
to a moving world.
home.journey.body: From quote to delivery, nothing on this site is typed in by hand. Every price, every date and every day-count on these pages is worked out by the same code a real system would run — change one input and everything downstream moves with it.
home.journey.bookingBody: The slot is held and the cut-offs start counting back from departure.
home.journey.deliveryBody: The container moves. Every container shipped counts towards the customer's next loyalty reward.
home.journey.quoteBody: Pick a lane, the containers and a day. Every line of the quotation is itemised.
home.journey.title:
End to end.
Every figure computed.
home.net.body: A shipping network only works if every port, every ship and every price agree with each other. This site models a small, honest slice of one — four ports, six lanes, and the pricing rules that connect them.
home.net.title: A connected global supply chain
home.persp.body: The same programme, read three ways. Start with whichever one is yours.
home.persp.businessBody: Quoting logic, lane pricing, and how TEU volume turns into tiered rewards.
home.persp.engineeringBody: What happens in the 1.3 seconds after a customer presses Quote — one screen per step.
home.persp.processBody: Two ways of delivering the same work — a two-week sprint, or one 72-hour cycle — and what each costs.
home.persp.title: Three ways in

Accept one and the ticket appears underneath. Change any input and every figure on the page follows.
home.platform.title:
Where it all
ends up
journey.arrival.body: The rate, the sailing, the charges and the validity are on the customer's screen. Tomorrow morning they can book at the same figure. No desk was involved, and none would have been at 2 a.m. either. That is not a reason to trust it less: a person looking at the same inputs would reach the same number, because the arithmetic is fixed and checked.
journey.arrival.fact: {ms} milliseconds, end to end. Not one of them was a person.
journey.arrival.label: Back on the customer's screen
journey.arrival.title: And it is back.
journey.erp-system.body: The computed rate is reserved in the core booking system for 72 hours. This is the step that turns a number on a screen into something a customer can act on: until it happens the quote is a display, and after it the quote is a hold.
journey.erp-system.fact: The 72-hour validity starts counting here, not when the customer reads it.
journey.erp-system.name: The hold
journey.erp-system.title: Space is held on the ship.
journey.lede: One request, five steps, and nobody at a desk. This is what the system does between a customer pressing the button and a rate coming back — one screen per step, in the order it happens. For scale: it is over before an email to a sales desk would have been opened.
journey.new-request.body: A customer picks an origin and a destination, lists the containers — type, how many, how heavy — names the commodity and picks a departure day from the calendar. Then presses Quote. That is the whole request; nothing else is asked for, because nothing else is needed to price it.
journey.new-request.fact: Five fields: where from, where to, which boxes, what is in them, which day. The same five whether it is a phone at 2 a.m. or a partner's system sending the request automatically.
journey.new-request.name: The request
journey.new-request.title: The request comes in.
journey.quotation-service.body: The lane's base rate, times the container's factor, times the number of boxes. Then handling per box, a documentation fee per shipment, a fuel surcharge as a share of the freight — and the loyalty tier's discount off the lot. Every line of the invoice on the Business page is born in these {ms} milliseconds.
journey.quotation-service.fact: Same inputs, same number, every time. The arithmetic cannot depend on who asks or when, and an automatic test checks it on every change.
journey.quotation-service.name: The price
journey.quotation-service.title: The price is worked out.
journey.request-intake.body: Do both ports exist? Does the cargo weight fit what each box can carry? Does the commodity need a reefer, and is one listed? Are origin and destination different places? A request that fails any of these stops here, with a message, and never reaches the pricing engine.
journey.request-intake.fact: A request with a mistake in it is stopped here, at the door, before anything downstream has spent time on it.
journey.request-intake.name: The check
journey.request-intake.title: It is checked before it goes anywhere.
journey.routing-gateway.body: Quotations go to the quotation team, campaigns to the campaign team. When a promotion makes quote traffic jump eightfold, this is the place that absorbs it — more copies of the quotation service are started to share the load, and the surge never reaches the systems behind it.
journey.routing-gateway.fact: The core booking system never feels a marketing campaign. That is what the split is for.
journey.routing-gateway.name: The hand-off
journey.routing-gateway.title: It is handed to the right team.
journey.title: {s} seconds after you press Quote.

node.analytics.role: Reporting over the Data Platform replica. Read-only, and deliberately downstream of everything.
node.api-integration.role: A partner system posts straight to the API. Same contract, same validation, no human keying.
node.campaign-service.role: Segments customers and targets offers. The Campaign Cohort Hub.
node.data-platform.role: The analytics store, fed from a read replica so reporting can never contend with booking writes.
node.email.role: A request arrives as free text and is parsed into the same intake payload, so nothing downstream ever learns which channel it came from.
node.erp-system.role: The Legacy ERP Engine. System of record for rates, bookings and reservations: everything transactional is ultimately true here or not true at all.
node.feature-flags.role: Decides which behaviour a given customer sees, so deploying and releasing stop being the same event.
node.new-request.role: A customer starts a rate request in the portal. The default entry point, and the one every other channel converges on.
node.notification-service.role: Fans the outcome out asynchronously, so a slow mail provider can never delay a quote response.
node.quotation-service.role: Prices a lane and reserves the resulting rate. The Core Quotation Module.
node.request-intake.role: Captures and normalises the request, whatever channel it arrived on, and hands one shape to the service layer.
node.request-tracker.role: The customer-facing status view. It reads request state; it never mutates it.
node.routing-gateway.role: The single front door. Everything the platform serves passes through here and is routed, rate-limited and traced.
node.translation-api.role: Supplies localised copy from outside the build, so wording can be corrected without a release.
node.validation.role: Schema, lane and eligibility checks run before anything is priced. A request that fails here never reaches the service layer.

persona.business.blurb: Quoting logic, lane pricing, and how TEU volume turns into tiered rewards.
persona.engineering.blurb: Service boundaries, request routing, and the trade-offs behind each layer.
persona.process.blurb: Two delivery models compared, then a knowledge check on the team's rules.
platform.body: Every service in stages 03 and 04 is a Deployment on a managed container platform. The Routing Gateway is the cluster ingress. The Quotation Service scales horizontally on p95 latency rather than CPU, because a slow rate reservation against the Legacy ERP Engine shows up as latency long before it shows up as load.
platform.title: Everything above runs on a managed cluster
process.ai.blurb: One Bolt. Four phases. Nobody to hand to.
process.ai.title: AI-DLC
process.forward.alt: A person stepping up a short flight of blocks towards a red panel.
process.forward.lede: The same agile principles, with the queues taken out. The one human step that remains is the judgement call.
process.hero.alt: A team at a planning board, work on the wall behind them.
process.lede: AI-DLC — the AI-Driven Life Cycle — does not make the five roles faster. It removes the line they stand in: one cycle, four phases, requirement to production, run by a small team of one to five people. The work was never slow — what took two weeks was the waiting between hands.
process.protocol.approvalsBody: A pull request needs at least two independent approvals. One reviewer is both a bottleneck and a single point of failure; branch protection enforces the count, and a green build alone never unlocks the merge.
process.protocol.branchesBody: Branch names carry their type and ticket, so the board and the repository can be reconciled without anybody maintaining a mapping by hand.
process.protocol.commitBody: Every commit opens with its ticket id. Release notes and the audit trail are generated from that tag, and a pre-receive hook rejects any subject line without one — the convention is enforced by the repository, not by reviewer goodwill.
process.protocol.lede: None of these depend on anybody remembering them, which is the only reason they hold under load. They are the rules in force today, on the scrum side of this page — and AI-DLC keeps the first two while replacing the third: the two-approval gate becomes Verification, a bot suite that runs the moment the code exists.
process.protocol.title: Three rules, enforced by tooling.
process.sim.alt: The floor plan: five desks in a row ending at a barrier, and one conveyor loop with a single desk beside it.
process.sim.lede: Five roles on one floor, four Bolt phases on the other. Drag a story point onto a station and watch where it stops — the queues are the argument, and they are there before you touch anything.
process.sim.title: Drop work into either floor.
process.title.a: The unit of work was two weeks.
process.trad.blurb: People build. Work waits between steps.
process.trad.title: Traditional scrum (AI assisted)
process.two.lede: People build in both. What differs is the unit of work: a sprint — a fixed two-week block passed between five roles — or a Bolt, AI-DLC's name for one cycle that closes inside 72 working hours.
process.two.title: Same work. Different flow.
process.why.gatesAlt: Two people working at their own desks, with a lowered barrier beside them.
process.why.gatesBody: A pull request needs two independent approvals, so it waits on two calendars rather than one.
process.why.handoffsAlt: One person holding out a box; the next has not turned round.
process.why.handoffsBody: Work is passed from one person to the next, and a queue forms at every boundary.
process.why.stagesAlt: One desk, one person, and boxes stacked all around it.
process.why.stagesBody: Each stage handles one item at a time, so a second item cannot flow in parallel — it queues.
process.why.title: Work waits because of the process, not the people.
quality.alt: One person adding a red cube to a wall of white ones.
quality.attr.post: . {note} Every figure in this band comes from that one place; nothing published is mixed into it.
quality.card.breakEven.body: Not measured — divided. If {n}× the defects are surfaced, a review gate has to stop four of every five just to put the release back where it was without an assistant. 1 − 1/{n}, and nothing else enters it.
quality.card.breakEven.title: What a gate must catch to break even
quality.card.defects.body: Same benchmark, same code. Detection, not injection: five times as many defects caught, which is the case for the gate rather than a charge against the assistant.
quality.card.defects.title: Defects found
quality.card.leadTime.body: From the proof-of-concept benchmark the team adopted with AI-DLC. Not this team's own delivery record — see below.
quality.card.leadTime.title: Throughput
quality.gap.body: The two numbers above — throughput ×{speed}, defects found ×{defects} — are a benchmark, not this team's record. The team's record exists: Jira holds every defect, task, assignee and resolution time, reported every two weeks. What it has not yet produced is a multiplier of its own, or a count of what Bot QA actually stopped on this team's delivery. So the {breakEven}% above is a target with nothing measured beside it, and this page cannot say whether it is reached. Other companies have measured their own gates, and those figures are worth reading — but they are theirs, so they stay out of this band.
quality.gap.title: What we cannot show you yet
quality.lede: Assistance does not make a team a little faster and a little sloppier. In the proof-of-concept the team adopted with AI-DLC, roughly three times as much got written and roughly five times as many defects were found in it. That is not a decline: finding them is what the automated review (Bot QA) is for, and redoing everything it stops is still paid for by the threefold speed. This is why AI-DLC puts a Bot gate where two human approvals used to be.
quality.modal.caption: The measurements these figures come from
quality.modal.gate.body: At our {factor}× injection rate a gate has to catch {breakEven}% to break even with writing the code by hand. The best catch rate anybody has published is {recovery}%, which would still ship {escape}× the defects of the unassisted baseline. Applying their rate to our rate is arithmetic across two different teams and it is not evidence about ours — it is the reason the target is worth stating at all.
quality.modal.gate.strong: And the best of them is not enough.
quality.modal.lede: No published study reports anything close to the POC figures. The benchmark is {speedGap}× the published median on throughput and {defectGap}× on defects. That gap is worth sitting with rather than explaining away: a proof of concept measures a chosen task under chosen conditions, and a study across 84 organisations measures the average — and the honest position is that neither is this team's own delivery.
quality.modal.title: What everyone else found
quality.poc.label: external POC benchmark
quality.poc.methodology: The two multipliers are from an external proof-of-concept benchmark; its sample size and counting method are not in this team's hands, so the figure cannot be reproduced from here — which is exactly why the published studies sit beside it. The team's own delivery is tracked: every defect, task, assignee and resolution time is in Jira, reported every two weeks. That record has not yet been reported as a multiplier.
quality.poc.note: The proof-of-concept the team referenced when adopting AI-DLC — not a measurement of this team's own delivery.
quality.title: Three times the throughput. Five times the defects found.
quiz.announceCorrect: Correct. The explanation is below, and the next question is ready.
quiz.announceWrong: Incorrect. The correct answer is {text}. The explanation is below.
quiz.full: Full marks. Every rule above is enforced by tooling rather than by memory, which is the point.
quiz.lede: Five questions on the rules this way of working runs on. Each answer explains why the rule exists, not only what it is.
quiz.q1.c: The branch name repeated as the subject line
quiz.q1.prompt: Under the Agile Delivery Protocol, which commit message structure is mandatory?
quiz.q1.why: Every commit stays traceable to a ticket. Release notes and audit trails are generated from the tag, and the pre-receive hook rejects any subject line that does not open with the ticket id — so the convention is enforced by the repository, not by reviewer goodwill.
quiz.q2.prompt: At what TEU milestone interval does a Blue Wave customer earn a performance reward?
quiz.q2.why: Blue Wave is the entry tier and carries no rate discount at all — its entire value is the coupon granted every 5 TEUs of accrued volume. Get the interval wrong and the whole entry-tier incentive is mispriced.
quiz.q3.c: None, provided the build is green
quiz.q3.prompt: How many peer approvals must a Pull Request carry before it can be merged?
quiz.q3.why: The Agile Delivery Protocol requires at least two independent approvals so that no single reviewer becomes a bottleneck or a single point of failure. Branch protection enforces it; a green build alone never unlocks the merge.
quiz.q4.c: One cubic metre of cargo volume
quiz.q4.prompt: In ocean freight capacity, what does one TEU represent?
quiz.q4.why: TEU is the normalising unit for the entire Volume Loyalty Framework. A 40' High Cube counts as 2 TEU, so five of them accrue 10 TEU rather than 5 — misreading this doubles or halves every reward calculation downstream.
quiz.q5.a: Issuing the final bill of lading
quiz.q5.c: Holding short-term freight rates across multiple ports so a customer can compare and book later
quiz.q5.d: Persisting booking records in the Legacy ERP Engine
quiz.q5.prompt: What is the Quotation Flex Cart responsible for?
quiz.q5.why: The Quotation Flex Cart is a rate-hold layer, not a booking system. It keeps quotes valid for a fixed window across several lanes; the transaction is only committed once the Legacy ERP Engine confirms the booking.
quiz.review: Review the ones you missed below. Each explanation says why the rule exists, not just what it is.

sim.mode.aiSub: One Bolt. Requirement to production inside 72 working hours.
sim.readout.caption: Simulated cycle time in days for each dropped work item under both delivery approaches.
sim.readout.empty: Drop a story point box onto a step, or select one and press Enter, to see how long the same work takes under each approach.
sim.readout.note1: Flow efficiency under Traditional Agile is the share of elapsed time that is actual work. It falls as the piece of work gets bigger, because waiting grows faster than the work does.
sim.readout.note2: These are modelled figures, not measurements — with one exception. The Bolt's cap, 72 working hours, is the lifecycle's own stated window rather than a constant chosen here; what is ours is that a working day is eight hours and that the largest item on the tray uses the whole window, with smaller ones in proportion. The traditional side is entirely a queueing model, and its four hand-off queues cost about two and a half days before any work starts, which is why the smallest item suffers the most. And the assumption carrying most of the difference is that Verification replaces the two-approval gate outright: if that gate stays human, the gap narrows sharply, which makes this an argument about the gate and not about the tooling.
sim.readout.title: Cycle time
sim.roles.note: Five roles on one side, four phases on the other, and that asymmetry is the point. A queue forms in front of a person, so the scrum floor is laid out by who holds the work — product owner, designer, developer, QA, and the two developers who must read the pull request. The Scrum Master is not a desk here: work never queues in front of them. The AI-DLC floor has no roles in a row at all, because inside one Bolt there is nobody to hand to.
sim.tray.group: Story points — the size of one piece of work
sim.tray.note: 0.5 is an afternoon; 8 is a fortnight for one person. Pick a size and drop it on a station to see how long it takes in each room.
sim.tray.title: Drop a piece of work in
station.bolt.does: Whatever passes ships. There is no release meeting to be scheduled into, which is the only reason a cycle can close inside 72 working hours at all.
station.bolt.name: The Bolt
station.construct.does: Two commits, not one. First the AI proposes the structure and the logic and a person reads it; only on approval does it write the code. This is the step that keeps the speed from becoming a liability.
station.construct.name: 2-PC Construct
station.design.does: Works out the screens and the states, then waits for a developer to be free.
station.design.name: Designer
station.dev.does: Writes the code, then hand-formats the commit to the [Ticket_ID] tag.
station.dev.name: Developer
station.inception.does: A person states the requirement and loads the context — house rules, design system, the graph of what touches what. Nothing is generated until this is right, because everything generated after it inherits it.
station.inception.name: Inception
station.po.does: Decides what the ticket means and what done looks like, then hands it on.
station.po.name: Product Owner
station.qa.does: Runs the checks by hand and re-reads the diff line by line.
station.qa.name: QA
station.review.does: Two other developers read the pull request. Neither of them was waiting for it, which is why this is the longest queue on the floor.
station.review.name: Two reviewers
station.verification.does: The bot suite runs the moment the code exists, edge cases included. This is what stands where two human approvals used to — not a shorter queue, a different mechanism.
station.verification.name: Verification

why.gradual.body: Multi-port rate holds went to five percent of Silver Sail customers before anyone else, with a switch that turns the feature off in seconds if the booking system slows down. Nothing else on the platform had to change for that to be possible.
why.gradual.title: A new feature can go to 5% of customers first
why.lede: None of them are about the technology. Each is a situation the company is in, and what the split lets it do about it.
why.night.body: Pricing needs no person, so it runs when nobody is there. The rate is held for 72 hours, so the customer who asked at night books at the same figure in the morning — no re-quote, no negotiation, no callback.
why.night.title: 2 a.m. gets the same answer as 2 p.m.
why.surge.body: When a campaign sends quote traffic up eightfold, only the quotation service is scaled up to meet it. The booking system behind it sees a steady stream, because the gateway in front of it is the thing that stretches.
why.surge.title: A promotion does not take the booking system down
why.title: Five services instead of one program, for three reasons the business would recognise.
